title: Clearance of a Contrast Agent from the Bloodstream
context: A radiology lab injects a bolus of iodine-based contrast agent and tracks how quickly the kidneys clear it from the blood. The concentration decays at a rate proportional to how much is currently present, a first-order elimination process you can hand straight to ode45.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The elimination rate constant is k = 0.15 per minute. Write an anonymous-function ODE handle f = @(t,C) ... representing dC/dt = -k*C.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using tspan = [0 30] and an initial concentration C0 = 8 (mg/L), call ode45 to solve for the concentration over time. Store the outputs as t and C.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot C versus t with axis labels 'Time (min)' and 'Concentration (mg/L)' and the title 'Contrast Agent Clearance'.

starterCode:
% Problem: Clearance of a Contrast Agent from the Bloodstream
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Define k and the ODE handle f = @(t,C) ...


% b) Solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 30], C0 = 8


% c) Plot C vs t with labels and title
hints: Every odefun handle for ode45 must accept exactly two inputs, t and the state (here just C), even though t never actually appears on the right-hand side of dC/dt = -k*C.
ode45 is called as [t, C] = ode45(f, tspan, C0) -- the function handle first, then the time span, then the initial condition.
Because this is a single first-order equation, C0 is just the scalar 8, and the output C will come back as a column vector the same length as t.
solutionExplanation: dC/dt = -k*C is the simplest kind of first-order ODE ode45 can solve: the derivative depends only on the current value of C, not explicitly on t, but MATLAB's odefun convention still requires the handle to accept both t and C as inputs. ode45 takes that handle, the time interval [0 30], and the scalar initial condition C0 = 8, and returns a column vector t of the (adaptively chosen) time points it evaluated at, along with the matching concentration values in C. Because k = 0.15 > 0 multiplies a negative sign, the concentration decays smoothly toward zero, which is exactly the exponential-decay shape you'd expect from first-order elimination kinetics -- the same behavior you could confirm analytically since this equation's exact solution is C(t) = C0*exp(-k*t).
concept: Setting up and calling ode45 for a single first-order ODE

title: Cooling of a Donor Organ in Transit
context: A donor organ is packed in an ice-slurry cooler at a fixed ambient temperature for transport. Newton's law of cooling says the organ's temperature approaches the ambient temperature at a rate proportional to the current temperature difference -- another single-equation ode45 setup, but this time with a nonzero forcing term inside the handle.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The cooling constant is k = 0.12 per minute and the ambient cooler temperature is Tamb = 4 (degrees C). Write the ODE handle f = @(t,T) ... representing dT/dt = -k*(T - Tamb).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using tspan = [0 45] and initial organ temperature T0 = 37, call ode45 to solve for T over time.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot T versus t with axis labels and the title 'Donor Organ Cooling Curve', then use fprintf to display the final temperature in T (the last entry) rounded to 1 decimal place.

starterCode:
% Problem: Cooling of a Donor Organ in Transit
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Define k, Tamb, and the ODE handle f = @(t,T) ...


% b) Solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 45], T0 = 37


% c) Plot, then display the final temperature with fprintf
hints: Tamb is a constant that belongs inside the handle's formula, not a second state variable -- the state being solved for is still just T, a single number at each time point.
T(end) gives you the last row of the solution vector T, which corresponds to the temperature at the final time in tspan.
Since Tamb = 4 is below the starting T0 = 37, the temperature should decrease and level off near 4 degrees C as t grows, never actually reaching it exactly within a finite time.
solutionExplanation: The handle f = @(t,T) -k*(T - Tamb) captures Newton's law of cooling: the rate of temperature change is proportional to how far T currently is from the ambient temperature, so the cooling slows down as T approaches Tamb rather than continuing at a constant rate. Passing this handle, tspan = [0 45], and T0 = 37 into ode45 produces a temperature curve that starts at body temperature and decays toward, but never quite reaches, the 4-degree ambient temperature over the 45-minute transport window. T(end) pulls out the very last computed temperature value, which for these parameters comes out just above 4 degrees C, reflecting that 45 minutes is long enough for the organ to have cooled almost all the way to the cooler's temperature.
concept: Calling ode45 for a first-order ODE with a constant forcing term

title: Building a State-Space Handle for a Two-Compartment IV Bolus
context: After an IV bolus, drug moves between the bloodstream and a peripheral tissue compartment. Before you can hand a coupled system to ode45, you need to package both equations into a single state vector and a single anonymous function -- the same first step every coupled ODE problem in this unit starts with.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The system is dx1/dt = -0.20*x1 + 0.05*x2 (blood) and dx2/dt = 0.15*x1 - 0.05*x2 (tissue), where x1 and x2 are drug amounts (mg). Define the state vector as s = [x1; x2] and write the combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...] returning both derivatives as a 2x1 column.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Define the initial condition vector s0 = [10; 0] (all drug starts in the blood). Without calling any solver yet, evaluate f(0, s0) directly and display the result -- this is exactly the derivative vector ode45 would use for its very first step.

starterCode:
% Problem: Building a State-Space Handle for a Two-Compartment IV Bolus
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

% a) Define the combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]


% b) Define s0 and evaluate f(0, s0); display the result
hints: Each row of the output vector corresponds to one compartment's equation -- row 1 must be dx1/dt using s(1) and s(2), row 2 must be dx2/dt using the same two entries.
Separate the two expressions with a semicolon inside the brackets, e.g. f = @(t,s) [expr1; expr2], so the handle returns a 2x1 column vector rather than a 1x2 row.
f(0, s0) just substitutes s(1) = 10 and s(2) = 0 into both formulas -- no loop or solver call is needed to compute this single derivative evaluation.
solutionCode:
% a) Combined state-space ODE handle
f = @(t, s) [-0.20 * s(1) + 0.05 * s(2); ...   % dx1/dt (blood)
              0.15 * s(1) - 0.05 * s(2)];      % dx2/dt (tissue)

% b) Initial condition and a single derivative evaluation
s0 = [10; 0];
initialDerivative = f(0, s0);
disp(initialDerivative)
solutionExplanation: Packaging a coupled system for ode45 always starts the same way: stack the individual state variables into one column vector s, then write a single handle whose output is a same-size column vector of derivatives, one row per equation. Here s(1) tracks blood drug amount and s(2) tracks tissue drug amount, so row 1 of f's output must be the blood equation and row 2 the tissue equation, each written in terms of s(1) and s(2) rather than x1 and x2 directly. Evaluating f(0, s0) with s0 = [10; 0] substitutes s(1)=10, s(2)=0 into both rows, giving [-0.20*10 + 0.05*0; 0.15*10 - 0.05*0] = [-2; 1.5] -- meaning that, at the instant the bolus is given, blood drug is falling at 2 mg/min while tissue drug is rising at 1.5 mg/min, which makes physical sense since all the drug starts in the blood and none has yet accumulated in the tissue.
concept: Formulating a coupled two-compartment system as a single state vector and ODE handle

title: Bacterial Growth in a Wound Culture

Over the short observation window before nutrients become limiting, the colony grows at a rate proportional to its current size -- exponential growth, one of the simplest physiological ODE models you can hand to ode45.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The growth rate constant is r = 0.4 per hour. Write the ODE handle f = @(t,N) ... representing dN/dt = r*N.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using tspan = [0 10] (hours) and an initial colony size N0 = 50 (CFU, arbitrary units), call ode45 to solve for N over time.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot N versus t with axis labels 'Time (hr)' and 'Colony size (CFU)' and the title 'Bacterial Growth in Wound Culture'.

starterCode:
% Problem: Bacterial Growth in a Wound Culture
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Define r and the ODE handle f = @(t,N) ...


% b) Solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 10], N0 = 50


% c) Plot N vs t with labels and title
hints: This is the same one-line pattern as any single-equation ode45 problem: define the rate constant, write f = @(t,N) r*N, then call [t,N] = ode45(f, tspan, N0).
Because there's no limiting term here (no carrying capacity), N will grow without bound over the 10-hour window rather than leveling off.
The shape of the resulting curve should look like unrestricted exponential growth -- it should curve upward increasingly steeply, not level off or decay.
solutionExplanation: dN/dt = r*N is the classic unconstrained exponential-growth model: the larger the colony currently is, the faster it grows, with no term that ever slows that growth down. Handing this handle, a 10-hour tspan, and the starting size N0 = 50 to ode45 produces a solution that climbs from 50 toward roughly 50*exp(0.4*10), about 2730 CFU, tracing the classic upward-curving exponential shape. This same equation form reappears constantly in physiological modeling -- viral load early in an infection, tumor growth before it outstrips its blood supply, or population growth before resources become scarce -- which is why it's worth recognizing on sight even before you look at the parameter values.
concept: Exponential growth as a single-equation ode45 model

title: Comparing tspan Formats for a Sedative Washout Curve
context: A sedative's blood concentration falls off after infusion stops, following simple first-order elimination. ode45 accepts tspan either as a two-element interval [t0 tf] (letting the solver pick its own adaptive time points) or as a longer vector of specific times you want reported -- this problem has you try both and see how the outputs differ.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: With k = 0.25 per hour and f = @(t,C) -k*C, call ode45 using tspan = [0 12] and C0 = 6. Store the results as t1, C1, and display length(t1).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Call ode45 again with the same f and C0, but this time use tspan = 0:1:12 (an explicit vector of hours 0 through 12). Store the results as t2, C2, and display length(t2).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In a one-line comment, explain why length(t1) and length(t2) come out different even though both calls solve the exact same differential equation over the exact same overall time range.

hints: A two-element tspan like [0 12] only tells ode45 the start and end times -- everything in between is chosen automatically by its adaptive step-size algorithm.

A longer tspan vector like 0:1:12 is instead treated as a specific list of times at which you're asking to see the solution -- ode45 still adapts its internal steps, but only reports back the values at exactly those requested points.

length(t2) should come out to exactly 13 (one value for each hour from 0 to 12), while length(t1) will typically be a different number determined by however many adaptive steps ode45 needed for this particular equation.
solutionExplanation: Both calls solve the identical equation dC/dt = -k*C from t=0 to t=12 with the same initial condition, so C1 and C2 agree at every time they share in common -- but the two tspan forms tell ode45 to report back differently. Passing tspan = [0 12] only specifies the start and end of the interval, so the adaptive Runge-Kutta stepping inside ode45 is free to choose however many intermediate points it judges necessary to keep the local error within tolerance, which is why length(t1) is whatever number the adaptive algorithm happened to need. Passing tspan = 0:1:12 instead gives ode45 a specific list of 13 output times; the solver still takes its own adaptive internal steps to get from one requested time to the next accurately, but it only returns the solution evaluated at those 13 points, so length(t2) is exactly 13 regardless of how many internal steps were actually taken.
concept: The difference between a two-element and vector-form tspan argument to ode45

title: A Simplified Host-Pathogen Population Model
context: An infectious-disease lab is tracking a simplified predator-prey-style interaction between a pathogen population and an immune-cell population that hunts it. You'll set up the coupled system, solve it, and interpret whether the two populations settle down or keep oscillating.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The pathogen population p and immune-cell population m follow dp/dt = 0.9*p - 0.4*p*m and dm/dt = -0.6*m + 0.2*p*m. Write the combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...] with s = [p; m].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Solve the system with ode45 over tspan = [0 30] and initial condition s0 = [4; 2]. Store the outputs as t and s.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot both p(t) (s(:,1)) and m(t) (s(:,2)) on the same axes, with a legend distinguishing 'Pathogen' and 'Immune cells', axis labels, and a title.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In 1-2 sentences, describe the qualitative pattern you see in the plot (do the two populations settle to constants, oscillate, or one wipe out the other?) and relate it to the predator-prey structure of the equations.

starterCode:
% Problem: A Simplified Host-Pathogen Population Model
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]


% b) Solve with ode45, tspan = [0 30], s0 = [4; 2]


% c) Plot both populations on one set of axes with a legend


% d) Written description of the qualitative pattern
hints: s(1) is the pathogen population p and s(2) is the immune-cell population m -- write each equation using only those two entries.

When ode45 returns a matrix output s (rather than separate p and m vectors), each state variable lives in its own column: s(:,1) is the full time history of p, and s(:,2) is the full time history of m.

This equation structure is the same predator-prey (Lotka-Volterra) form seen in Lecture 16 -- expect the two populations to rise and fall in a repeating, out-of-phase cycle rather than settling to fixed values.
solutionCode:
% a) Combined ODE handle
f = @(t, s) [0.9 * s(1) - 0.4 * s(1) * s(2); ...   % dp/dt
            -0.6 * s(2) + 0.2 * s(1) * s(2)];      % dm/dt

% b) Solve with ode45
tspan = [0 30];
s0 = [4; 2];
[t, s] = ode45(f, tspan, s0);

% c) Plot both populations
figure
plot(t, s(:,1), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t, s(:,2), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (days)')
ylabel('Population')
legend('Pathogen', 'Immune cells', 'Location', 'best')
title('Host-Pathogen Population Dynamics')

% d) Written description:
% Both populations rise and fall in a repeating, out-of-phase cycle rather
% than settling to constants -- the pathogen surges first, which feeds
% growth in immune cells, which in turn suppresses the pathogen and then
% declines again once its food source (the pathogen) is depleted, the
% classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey oscillation.
solutionExplanation: This system has the exact Lotka-Volterra predator-prey structure from Lecture 16: the pathogen (prey-like) grows on its own via the 0.9*p term but is suppressed by encounters with immune cells via -0.4*p*m, while the immune-cell population (predator-like) decays on its own via -0.6*m but grows from those same encounters via +0.2*p*m. Solving this with ode45 over 30 days from s0 = [4; 2] produces sustained, out-of-phase oscillations in both s(:,1) and s(:,2) rather than either population settling to a fixed value or one driving the other to extinction -- a pathogen surge is followed by a lagged rise in immune cells, which then drives the pathogen back down, after which the immune-cell population itself declines from lack of pathogen to respond to, and the cycle restarts. Recognizing this pattern matters clinically: it's the same qualitative signature (cyclic rather than monotonic) that shows up in real relapsing-infection dynamics, distinct from a system that cleanly resolves to a steady state.
concept: Coupled nonlinear (Lotka-Volterra-style) ODE systems and interpreting oscillatory behavior

title: Two-Compartment Oral Drug Absorption
context: After swallowing a pill, a drug first sits in the gut before crossing into the bloodstream, where it's eventually eliminated. You'll model this as a two-compartment linear system, solve it, and find when the blood concentration peaks -- a key quantity (Tmax) reported for every real oral drug.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Let g be the amount in the gut and b the amount in the blood, following dg/dt = -0.5*g and db/dt = 0.5*g - 0.2*b. Write the ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...] with s = [g; b].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 24] (hours) and initial condition s0 = [100; 0] (all 100 mg starts in the gut). Store the outputs as t and s.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot both g(t) and b(t) on the same axes with a legend, axis labels, and a title.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using max on the blood column of s, find the peak blood amount and the time at which it occurs (Tmax). Display both with fprintf.

starterCode:
% Problem: Two-Compartment Oral Drug Absorption
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]


% b) Solve with ode45, tspan = [0 24], s0 = [100; 0]


% c) Plot both g(t) and b(t) with a legend


% d) Find and display the peak blood amount and Tmax
hints: s(1) is gut amount g and s(2) is blood amount b -- the gut equation only depends on g itself, while the blood equation depends on both.
max() can return two outputs at once: [peakValue, peakIndex] = max(s(:,2)) gives you both the peak amount and the row where it occurred.
Once you have peakIndex, the corresponding time is simply t(peakIndex) -- the same row position in the time vector.
solutionCode:
% a) Combined ODE handle
f = @(t, s) [-0.5 * s(1); ...                  % dg/dt (gut)
              0.5 * s(1) - 0.2 * s(2)];        % db/dt (blood)

% b) Solve with ode45
tspan = [0 24];
s0 = [100; 0];
[t, s] = ode45(f, tspan, s0);

% c) Plot both compartments
figure
plot(t, s(:,1), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t, s(:,2), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (hr)')
ylabel('Amount (mg)')
legend('Gut', 'Blood', 'Location', 'best')
title('Two-Compartment Oral Drug Absorption')

% d) Find the peak blood amount and Tmax
[peakAmount, peakIndex] = max(s(:,2));
Tmax = t(peakIndex);
fprintf('Peak blood amount: %.2f mg at Tmax = %.2f hr\n', peakAmount, Tmax);
solutionExplanation: The gut compartment g decays purely on its own (dg/dt = -0.5*g), acting as the drug's source, while the blood compartment b gains drug from the gut's decay and loses it to elimination (db/dt = 0.5*g - 0.2*b), so b first rises while the gut still holds a large reservoir and then falls once the gut supply has mostly emptied and elimination dominates. This rise-then-fall shape is exactly why oral drug concentrations always show a peak rather than either monotonically rising or monotonically falling. [peakAmount, peakIndex] = max(s(:,2)) locates both the largest blood amount reached and the row of the solution array where that maximum occurred, and t(peakIndex) converts that row index into the actual time (Tmax) it happened at -- for these parameters, Tmax comes out to a few hours in, consistent with typical oral-drug absorption profiles where blood levels peak well before all the gut drug has transferred.
concept: Two-compartment absorption/elimination pharmacokinetics and locating a peak (Tmax) numerically

title: Tightening ode45's Tolerances for a Fast-Decaying Signal
context: A biosensor's raw voltage decays quickly after a stimulus pulse. ode45's default error tolerances are fine for most systems, but for equations with fast initial dynamics, tightening RelTol and AbsTol via odeset can noticeably change both the solution's accuracy and how many points ode45 reports.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For dV/dt = -5*V with V0 = 10 over tspan = [0 3], solve using ode45 with default tolerances. Store the results as t1, V1, and display length(t1).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using odeset, create an options structure with 'RelTol' set to 1e-8 and 'AbsTol' set to 1e-10. Solve the same equation again, passing options as the fourth argument to ode45. Store the results as t2, V2, and display length(t2).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare V1(end) and V2(end) (the final values from each run) by displaying their absolute difference. Comment in one line on whether tightening the tolerance changed the final answer meaningfully for this simple equation.

hints: odeset takes name-value pairs, e.g. options = odeset('RelTol', 1e-8, 'AbsTol', 1e-10), and returns a single options structure you pass along.
ode45 accepts an optional fourth argument for options: [t, V] = ode45(f, tspan, V0, options).

Tighter tolerances generally force ode45 to take more, smaller steps to stay within the stricter error bound, so expect length(t2) to be noticeably larger than length(t1) even though both solve the identical equation.
solutionExplanation: odeset('RelTol', 1e-8, 'AbsTol', 1e-10) builds an options structure that tells ode45 to keep its per-step error estimate below a much stricter bound than the defaults (RelTol = 1e-3, AbsTol = 1e-6), and passing that structure as the fourth argument to ode45 changes how carefully -- and therefore how often -- the solver steps forward. Because dV/dt = -5*V is a smooth, simple exponential decay with no sudden dynamics, the default tolerance already tracks the true solution quite well, so length(t2) is larger than length(t1) (more steps were taken to satisfy the tighter bound) but finalDiff, the difference between the two final values, is tiny. This illustrates a general lesson about tolerances: tightening them costs more computation but is only worth it when the extra accuracy is actually needed -- for a well-behaved equation like this one, the default settings were already good enough.
concept: Adjusting ode45's error tolerances with odeset and evaluating whether it changes the result

title: State-Space Form for a Tendon-Loading Model
context: A biomechanics lab models a tendon under a sudden load as a simple mass-spring system: the tendon's attached mass oscillates according to Newton's second law with a spring-like restoring force. Since this is a second-order equation, you'll first convert it into a two-state system before ode45 can touch it.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The governing equation is m*d2x/dt2 = -k*x, with m = 2 kg and k = 50 N/m. Define the state vector s = [x; dx/dt] = [s1; s2], and derive ds2/dt in terms of s1 and s2.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...] implementing the two-state system from (a), then solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 5] and initial condition s0 = [0.05; 0] (5 cm initial displacement, at rest).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot displacement (s(:,1)) and velocity (s(:,2)) on the same axes with a legend, axis labels, and a title.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In one sentence, describe how the displacement and velocity curves relate to each other over time (e.g., where is velocity zero relative to the displacement extremes?).

starterCode:
% Problem: State-Space Form for a Tendon-Loading Model
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

m = 2;   % kg
k = 50;  % N/m

% a) Derive ds2/dt in terms of s1 and s2 (write as a comment)


% b) ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]; solve with ode45, tspan = [0 5], s0 = [0.05; 0]


% c) Plot displacement and velocity with a legend


% d) One-sentence written description
hints: Rearranging m*d2x/dt2 = -k*x gives d2x/dt2 = -(k/m)*x -- substitute s1 for x, so ds2/dt = -(k/m)*s1.
The first row of f is always the easy one for this kind of conversion: ds1/dt = s2, since s2 was defined as the derivative of s1.

Because there's no damping term in this model, expect x(t) to oscillate indefinitely as a clean sine/cosine wave rather than decaying -- velocity should be zero exactly at the peaks and troughs of displacement.
solutionCode:
m = 2;   % kg
k = 50;  % N/m

% a) ds2/dt = -(k/m)*s1  (derived from m*d2x/dt2 = -k*x with s1 = x, s2 = dx/dt)

% b) Combined ODE handle and solve
f = @(t, s) [s(2); ...                  % ds1/dt = s2
            -(k/m) * s(1)];             % ds2/dt = -(k/m)*s1
tspan = [0 5];
s0 = [0.05; 0];
[t, s] = ode45(f, tspan, s0);

% c) Plot displacement and velocity
figure
plot(t, s(:,1), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t, s(:,2), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (s)')
ylabel('Displacement (m) / Velocity (m/s)')
legend('Displacement', 'Velocity', 'Location', 'best')
title('Tendon-Loading Mass-Spring Response')

% d) Written description:
% Velocity crosses zero exactly at each displacement peak and trough, and
% is largest in magnitude when displacement itself crosses zero -- the
% two curves are a quarter-cycle out of phase, as expected for undamped
% simple harmonic motion.
solutionExplanation: Converting the second-order equation m*d2x/dt2 = -k*x into state form follows the recipe from Lecture 15: with s1 = x and s2 = dx/dt, the first equation ds1/dt = s2 is automatic by definition, and the second comes from solving the original equation for the highest derivative, d2x/dt2 = -(k/m)*x, then substituting state variables to get ds2/dt = -(k/m)*s1. With m = 2 and k = 50, this describes undamped simple harmonic motion with angular frequency sqrt(k/m) = 5 rad/s, so ode45 produces a displacement s(:,1) that oscillates sinusoidally between +/-0.05 m and a velocity s(:,2) that is a quarter-cycle out of phase with it -- velocity is exactly zero whenever displacement is at a peak or trough (the mass has momentarily stopped to reverse direction), and velocity is at its own maximum magnitude whenever displacement passes through zero (the mass is moving fastest through its equilibrium point).
concept: Converting a second-order mechanical ODE into a two-state system and interpreting the phase relationship between position and velocity

title: A Minimal Glucose-Insulin Feedback Model

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot both g(t) and i(t) on the same axes with a legend, axis labels, and a title.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using min, find the lowest value glucose reaches over the simulation and the time at which it occurs. Display both with fprintf.

starterCode:

% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Combined ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]


% b) Solve with ode45, tspan = [0 20], s0 = [50; 0]

% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

% a) ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]; s0 = [3; 1.5]


% b) Solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 2000]; time it, display length(t)

hints: tic starts a stopwatch and toc reports (and can return) the elapsed time since the matching tic -- wrap just the ode45 or ode15s call itself, not any of the setup code, so the timing reflects only the solve.
ode15s is called with exactly the same argument order as ode45: [t, s] = ode15s(f, tspan, s0) -- no changes to the handle or initial condition are needed.
Expect ode45's length(t) to be dramatically larger than ode15s's for this system -- that gap in step count, not just the elapsed time, is the real signature of stiffness.

% Problem: Underdamped vs Overdamped Response in an RLC Vessel-Wall Analog
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

omega = 2;

% a) Parameterized ODE handle f = @(t,s,alpha) [...; ...]


% b) Underdamped (alpha = 0.3) -> t_u, s_u


% c) Overdamped (alpha = 3) -> t_o, s_o


% d) Plot i(t) for both cases with a legend


% e) Count zero-crossings in each using sign and diff
hints: Converting the second-order equation follows the same recipe every time: s1 = i, s2 = di/dt, so ds1/dt = s2 always, and ds2/dt comes from solving the original equation for the highest derivative: d2i/dt2 = -2*alpha*s2 - omega^2*s1.
sign(i) returns -1, 0, or 1 depending on the sign of each entry; diff(sign(i)) is nonzero exactly at the positions where consecutive entries have different signs, i.e. where the curve crossed zero.

What alpha controls is the character of the response relative to omega: when alpha is small compared to omega (alpha = 0.3 versus omega = 2), the system is underdamped and oscillates back and forth across zero repeatedly as it decays, producing several zero-crossings. When alpha is large compared to omega (alpha = 3), the system is overdamped and the restoring force is overwhelmed by damping before it can overshoot past equilibrium even once, so i(t) decays smoothly toward zero without ever crossing it, giving zero crossings. This is the same underdamped/overdamped/critically-damped classification used throughout physiology wherever a compliant, damped structure responds to a pulse -- a healthy, appropriately damped vessel wall settles quickly without ringing, while an underdamped one continues to oscillate long after the initiating pressure pulse has passed.

% Date:

% c) Fast release (ka = 15) -> t_f, s_f

                  ka * s(1) - (ke + k12) * s(2) + k21 * s(3); ...  % dblood/dt
                  k12 * s(2) - k21 * s(3)];                        % dtissue/dt

tspan = [0 24];
s0 = [100; 0; 0];

% c) Fast release

[t_f, s_f] = ode45(fFast, tspan, s0);

% d) Plot blood concentration for both
figure
plot(t_n, s_n(:,2), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t_f, s_f(:,2), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (hr)')
ylabel('Blood amount (mg)')
legend('Normal release (ka = 1.5)', 'Fast release (ka = 15)', 'Location', 'best')
title('Blood Drug Levels: Normal vs Fast-Release Formulation')

[peakF, idxF] = max(s_f(:,2));
fprintf('Normal release: peak blood = %.2f mg at Tmax = %.2f hr\n', peakN, t_n(idxN));
fprintf('Fast release: peak blood = %.2f mg at Tmax = %.2f hr\n', peakF, t_f(idxF));

% A time constant of 1/ka is under 4 minutes for ka = 15, meaning the gut
% compartment would have to empty almost completely within a few minutes
% of swallowing the tablet. Real oral tablets must first dissolve and
% then cross the intestinal wall, a process that realistically takes on
% the order of tens of minutes to a couple of hours, not minutes -- so
% ka = 15 is not a plausible absorption rate for a swallowed pill. A gut
% compartment emptying that fast is more characteristic of a route that
% skips gut absorption altogether, such as an IV bolus or a sublingual
% (under-the-tongue) formulation that's absorbed directly through oral
% mucosa, rather than an actual 'fast-release' oral tablet.
solutionExplanation: Both formulations share identical elimination and distribution rates, so the comparison isolates exactly what changing the absorption rate constant ka does to the blood concentration profile: with ka = 1.5, blood levels rise over a couple of hours to a peak of roughly 61 mg around Tmax = 1.2 hours, while with ka = 15, blood levels spike to a much higher peak of roughly 90 mg within about 15 minutes (Tmax = 0.24 hours). While the model runs without any numerical difficulty at either value -- ode45 doesn't care whether ka is physiologically sensible -- the exercise's real point is that a model can be mathematically well-posed while still describing a physical situation that couldn't actually happen. A rate constant implying the gut essentially empties within minutes ignores the real time it takes a tablet to dissolve and for drug to cross the intestinal wall into the bloodstream, so this parameter regime is better interpreted as describing a different route of administration (IV or sublingual) rather than validating the 'fast-release oral tablet' framing it was given. Recognizing when a parameter value falls outside a model's realistic operating range -- not just whether the solver converges -- is an essential final check on any physiological ODE model.

% d) Plot tumor size for both
figure
plot(t_b, s_b(:,1), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t_w, s_w(:,1), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (days)')
ylabel('Tumor size T')
legend('Baseline immune response', 'Weakened immune response', 'Location', 'best')
title('Tumor-Immune Dynamics: Baseline vs Weakened Response')

% e) Final tumor size for each
fprintf('Baseline final tumor size: %.2f\n', s_b(end,1));
fprintf('Weakened final tumor size: %.2f\n', s_w(end,1));

% f) Written comparison:
% The baseline scenario settles to a tumor size of about 16.7, well below
% the carrying capacity of 100 -- the immune system is clearly still
% suppressing growth to a small, stable equilibrium. The weakened
% scenario settles to about 50, three times larger but still well short
% of the carrying capacity of 100. This means even the 'weakened' immune
% response in this model isn't a total failure: it still holds the tumor
% to roughly half of its unconstrained size rather than letting it
% escape to full carrying capacity, representing a partially effective
% but clearly degraded state of immune surveillance rather than complete
% immune evasion.
solutionExplanation: The logistic growth term r*T*(1 - T/K) alone would drive the tumor toward the carrying capacity K = 100, but the immune-kill term -c*T*I pulls it down, and how far it pulls depends on how much immune cell activity a_im sustains at equilibrium. With a_im = 0.05, immune cells are recruited quickly enough in response to tumor burden that the coupled system settles to a small stable tumor size around 16.7 -- a state of immune-mediated control. With a_im reduced to 0.01, immune cells are recruited five times more slowly, so less immune pressure builds up per unit of tumor, and the system instead settles at a much larger stable tumor size around 50. The key synthesis point is that 'weakened immune response' in this model does not mean the tumor escapes control entirely (T does not approach K = 100 in either case) -- it means the equilibrium point itself shifts to a larger, still-bounded tumor size, which is a biologically meaningful distinction: real tumor immunology recognizes intermediate states of partial immune control (tumor dormancy at an elevated burden) that are qualitatively different from either full clearance or complete immune escape, and this simplified model happens to reproduce that same three-way distinction from just one changed parameter.
concept: Synthesizing a nonlinear tumor-immune competition model and interpreting parameter-dependent equilibria in a biological context

title: Diagnosing Stiffness from Fast Enzyme-Substrate Binding
context: An enzyme binds and unbinds its substrate very quickly compared to how slowly it converts bound substrate into product. This kind of separation of timescales -- fast binding equilibrium, slow catalysis -- is a textbook source of numerical stiffness. You'll build the model, compare solvers, test whether tightening ode45's tolerance helps, and explain what's really going on.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Let s = [substrate; complex]. With fast binding/unbinding rate kon = koff = 500 and slow catalytic rate kcat = 0.5, write the ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...] implementing dsubstrate/dt = -kon*substrate + (koff+kcat)*complex and dcomplex/dt = kon*substrate - (koff+kcat)*complex, with s0 = [10; 0].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using tic/toc, solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 20]. Display the elapsed time and length(t).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using tic/toc, solve with ode15s over the same tspan. Display the elapsed time and length(t).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Re-solve with ode45 using odeset to tighten RelTol to 1e-6 and AbsTol to 1e-9, again timed with tic/toc. Display the elapsed time and length(t), and compare this step count to the default-tolerance ode45 run from (b).

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: In a short written comment, explain why this system is stiff in terms of the two rate constants involved, and explain why tightening ode45's tolerance in part (d) did NOT meaningfully close the step-count gap with ode15s from part (c).

starterCode:
% Problem: Diagnosing Stiffness from Fast Enzyme-Substrate Binding
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc;

kon = 500; koff = 500; kcat = 0.5;

% a) ODE handle f = @(t,s) [...; ...]; s0 = [10; 0]


% b) Solve with ode45, tspan = [0 20], timed with tic/toc; display length(t)


% c) Solve with ode15s, same tspan, timed; display length(t)


% d) Re-solve with ode45 using tightened odeset tolerances, timed; display length(t)


% e) Written explanation of stiffness and why tightening tolerance didn't help
hints: The two timescales here are 1/kon (roughly how fast binding equilibrium is reached) and 1/kcat (roughly how fast the slow catalytic conversion happens) -- compare their orders of magnitude.

odeset('RelTol', 1e-6, 'AbsTol', 1e-9) followed by passing that structure as ode45's fourth argument tightens the accuracy requirement without changing anything about the underlying stiffness of the problem.

A nonstiff explicit solver like ode45 must keep its step size small enough for numerical stability near the fast timescale everywhere in the simulation, even during the long slow-catalysis stretch -- tightening tolerance changes how accurate each step must be, but doesn't remove that stability-driven step-size ceiling, which is set by the fast rate constant regardless of tolerance.
solutionExplanation: The two rate constants kon/koff = 500 and kcat = 0.5 differ by three orders of magnitude, meaning the substrate-complex binding reaction equilibrates almost instantly (on a timescale of milliseconds) while the actual catalytic turnover into product happens on a timescale of seconds -- exactly the kind of multi-timescale separation that defines a stiff system. ode45's explicit Runge-Kutta stepping must stay small enough to remain numerically stable near the fast mode throughout the whole 20-time-unit simulation, even during the long stretch where the system has already settled into its slow-catalysis behavior, which is why it needs tens of thousands of steps. Tightening RelTol and AbsTol in part (d) makes ode45 demand a more accurate answer at each step, but it does nothing to relax the stability-driven step-size ceiling imposed by the fast timescale -- so the step count barely budges, confirming that ode45's struggle here is a stability problem, not an accuracy problem. ode15s solves this by using an implicit method whose stability doesn't depend on resolving the fast mode at every step, letting it take orders-of-magnitude larger steps and finish in a fraction of the steps -- which is the real lesson Lecture 14's stiffness discussion is pointing at: when a nonstiff solver needs a suspiciously large number of steps, the fix is switching solver families, not tightening tolerance.
concept: Diagnosing numerical stiffness from disparate rate constants, and distinguishing accuracy-driven from stability-driven step-size limits

title: Windkessel Model of Arterial Pressure Under Vasodilatory Shock
context: A two-compartment Windkessel model represents the arterial and venous sides of the circulation, each with its own compliance, connected by a resistance that a doctor can think of as systemic vascular resistance. You'll simulate a normal resting patient and a patient in vasodilatory (septic) shock, where systemic vascular resistance collapses, and assess whether the resulting pressures are consistent with real clinical danger signs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Let s = [Pa; Pv] (arterial, venous pressure). With cardiac output baseline Q0 = 5, arterial compliance Ca = 0.03, venous compliance Cv = 0.3, venous resistance Rv = 1, and heart rate omega = 2*pi*1.2 fixed, write a parameterized ODE handle f = @(t,s,R) [...; ...] implementing dPa/dt = (1/Ca)*(Q0*(1+sin(omega*t)) - (Pa-Pv)/R) and dPv/dt = (1/Cv)*((Pa-Pv)/R - Pv/Rv), where R is the systemic vascular resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Wrap f with R = 17 (normal resistance) and solve with ode45 over tspan = [0 10] and s0 = [90; 5]. Store as t_n, s_n.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Wrap f with R = 3 (severe vasodilation) and solve the same way. Store as t_s, s_s.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Plot arterial pressure Pa(t) (column 1) for both cases on the same axes with a legend.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: For each case, using only the portion of the solution where t > 8 (to look at the settled, steady periodic behavior), find the minimum and maximum arterial pressure and display the resulting pressure range and mean for each with fprintf.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: In a short written comment, compare both steady-state pressure ranges to a normal resting human arterial pressure of roughly 70-120 mmHg, and discuss whether the R = 3 scenario represents a physiologically dangerous state, tying your answer to what R = 3 represents clinically.

starterCode:
% Problem: Windkessel Model of Arterial Pressure Under Vasodilatory Shock
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

Q0 = 5; Ca = 0.03; Cv = 0.3; Rv = 1; omega = 2*pi*1.2;

% a) Parameterized ODE handle f = @(t,s,R) [...; ...]


% b) Normal resistance (R = 17) -> t_n, s_n


% c) Severe vasodilation (R = 3) -> t_s, s_s


% d) Plot Pa(t) for both cases with a legend


% e) Steady-state (t > 8) min/max/mean arterial pressure for each, via fprintf


% f) Written comparison to normal pressure range and clinical discussion
hints: Logical indexing works the same way here as anywhere else: s_n(t_n > 8, 1) pulls out only the arterial pressure values from rows where the corresponding time exceeds 8.
min and max applied to that filtered slice give the steady-state pressure range directly; mean() on the same slice gives the average pressure once transients have died out.

R represents systemic vascular resistance -- a very low R means blood vessels have lost their ability to constrict, which is exactly the mechanism behind vasodilatory (septic) shock, where blood pressure can fall dangerously even though the heart itself is still pumping normally.
solutionCode:
Q0 = 5; Ca = 0.03; Cv = 0.3; Rv = 1; omega = 2*pi*1.2;

% a) Parameterized two-compartment Windkessel ODE handle
f = @(t, s, R) [(1/Ca) * (Q0 * (1 + sin(omega*t)) - (s(1) - s(2)) / R); ...  % dPa/dt
                (1/Cv) * ((s(1) - s(2)) / R - s(2) / Rv)];                   % dPv/dt

% b) Normal systemic vascular resistance
fNormal = @(t, s) f(t, s, 17);
tspan = [0 10];
s0 = [90; 5];
[t_n, s_n] = ode45(fNormal, tspan, s0);

% c) Severe vasodilation
fShock = @(t, s) f(t, s, 3);
[t_s, s_s] = ode45(fShock, tspan, s0);

% d) Plot arterial pressure for both
figure
plot(t_n, s_n(:,1), 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold on
plot(t_s, s_s(:,1), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
hold off
xlabel('Time (s)')
ylabel('Arterial pressure (mmHg)')
legend('Normal (R = 17)', 'Vasodilatory shock (R = 3)', 'Location', 'best')
title('Windkessel Arterial Pressure: Normal vs Vasodilatory Shock')

% e) Steady-state pressure range and mean for each
Pa_n_tail = s_n(t_n > 8, 1);
Pa_s_tail = s_s(t_s > 8, 1);
fprintf('Normal: Pa ranges %.1f to %.1f mmHg (mean %.1f)\n', min(Pa_n_tail), max(Pa_n_tail), mean(Pa_n_tail));
fprintf('Shock: Pa ranges %.1f to %.1f mmHg (mean %.1f)\n', min(Pa_s_tail), max(Pa_s_tail), mean(Pa_s_tail));

% f) Written comparison:
% The normal scenario settles to an arterial pressure oscillating
% roughly between 69 and 111 mmHg (mean around 90), squarely within the
% normal resting range of about 70-120 mmHg. The R = 3 shock scenario
% settles to a much lower range, roughly 8 to 32 mmHg -- well below even
% the low end of the normal range, and consistent with severe, likely
% life-threatening hypotension. R represents systemic vascular
% resistance, and a value this low corresponds to blood vessels that
% have lost most of their ability to constrict, exactly the mechanism
% behind vasodilatory (septic) shock, where the heart may still be
% pumping an adequate cardiac output (Q0 was left unchanged here) but
% blood pressure collapses anyway because the vessels can no longer
% maintain resistance against that flow.
solutionExplanation: The Windkessel model splits the circulation into two compliant compartments connected by a resistance R: the arterial side receives pulsatile inflow from the heart (Q0*(1+sin(omega*t))) and loses pressure across R toward the venous side, while the venous side receives that same flow and loses it across its own resistance Rv. With normal resistance (R = 17), the model settles into a steady periodic oscillation with arterial pressure cycling between roughly 69 and 111 mmHg around a mean of about 90 mmHg -- a textbook-realistic systolic/diastolic-like swing. Dropping R to 3 to simulate the loss of vascular tone seen in vasodilatory shock causes the arterial pressure to collapse to a range of roughly 8 to 32 mmHg, since the same cardiac output can no longer generate adequate pressure once the vessels have lost most of their resistance to flow. The key synthesis insight is that this pressure collapse happens even though cardiac output (Q0) was never changed -- it's a pure consequence of the resistance term, which is exactly why vasodilatory shock is treated clinically with vasopressor drugs that restore vessel tone (effectively raising R back up) rather than only with fluids or drugs that increase cardiac output, since the model shows that pumping harder cannot by itself compensate for vessels that have lost their ability to constrict.
concept: Synthesizing a forced two-compartment cardiovascular model and evaluating steady-state output against real physiological reference ranges

title: When Does a Respiratory Oscillator Stop Looking Like Breathing?
context: The Van der Pol oscillator is sometimes used as a toy model for a self-sustaining biological rhythm, such as a respiratory central pattern generator producing a periodic breathing drive signal. You'll sweep its nonlinearity parameter across a wide range and assess at what point the oscillation stops resembling a smooth, physiologically plausible breathing rhythm.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write a parameterized ODE handle f = @(t,s,mu) [...; ...] implementing the Van der Pol system ds1/dt = s2 and ds2/dt = mu*(1 - s1^2)*s2 - s1, with s0 = [2; 0].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using a for-loop over mu = [0.5, 3, 15], solve the system with ode45 for each value over tspan = [0 60], storing each solution's t and s(:,1) (call them v) in a cell array.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot v(t) for all three mu values on the same axes with a legend showing each mu value.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: For each mu, use islocalmax on v to find the peak times, then use diff on those peak times to estimate the average oscillation period. Display all three average periods with fprintf.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: In a short written comment, describe how the waveform's shape changes as mu increases from 0.5 to 15 (comparing period length and how sinusoidal versus 'sharp jump followed by slow ramp' each trace looks), and discuss whether the mu = 15 regime still looks like a plausible model of smooth, periodic breathing.

starterCode:
% Problem: When Does a Respiratory Oscillator Stop Looking Like Breathing?
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Parameterized ODE handle f = @(t,s,mu) [...; ...]; s0 = [2; 0]


% b) For-loop over mu = [0.5, 3, 15]; solve each with ode45, tspan = [0 60]


% c) Plot v(t) for all three mu values with a legend


% d) For each mu, estimate the average period using islocalmax and diff


% e) Written description of waveform shape change and plausibility discussion
hints: A cell array can hold results of different sizes -- results{k}.t and results{k}.v (or simply two separate cell arrays tAll{k}, vAll{k}) let you store each mu's solution without needing every solution to have the same number of rows.
islocalmax(v) applied to a full time series returns a logical vector marking every local peak; indexing t with that logical vector, t(islocalmax(v)), gives you just the times those peaks occurred.

As mu grows large, the Van der Pol oscillator transitions into a 'relaxation oscillation' regime: long slow drifts punctuated by fast, sharp jumps, and the period grows roughly in proportion to mu -- very different from the near-sinusoidal shape seen at small mu.
solutionExplanation: The parameterized handle lets a single for-loop sweep mu across [0.5, 3, 15] without rewriting the ODE definition each time, and storing each run's time and v(t) in cell arrays keeps the three (differently-sized) solutions organized for plotting and analysis afterward. islocalmax(v) identifies every local peak in each trace, and taking diff of the resulting peak times estimates the average time between consecutive breaths (the oscillation period) for each mu -- which grows from about 6.4 seconds at mu = 0.5 to about 8.9 seconds at mu = 3 to about 27 seconds at mu = 15, nearly a fourfold increase across the sweep. This lengthening period reflects a real qualitative transition in the Van der Pol oscillator: at small mu the system behaves like a nearly linear, sinusoidal oscillator, but at large mu it becomes a relaxation oscillator dominated by slow, gradual drift phases interrupted by fast, discontinuous-looking jumps between extremes. The synthesis question this problem is really asking is whether the model still describes the physiology it was proposed for -- and the answer is that it doesn't: a real central pattern generator driving breathing produces a period on the order of a few seconds with a comparatively smooth, rounded waveform, so the mu = 15 regime, despite being a perfectly valid mathematical solution to a valid-looking system, represents a parameter combination that has drifted outside the range where the model still means what it was built to mean.
concept: Parameter sweeps over a nonlinear oscillator, quantifying period via peak detection, and assessing model plausibility outside a realistic parameter range
